title: Conversation-turn batching frontier: latency vs cost for session workloads (Oct 2026)
body:
Summary:
This note explores the latency-cost frontier for conversational workloads when batching policies are conditioned on conversation turn properties (turn length, recency, and cache hit probability). The goal is to provide a small set of recommended runtime knobs and a compact visual/textual representation of tradeoffs that can be used in product-facing collateral and SRE runbooks.

Key takeaways (TL;DR):
- Conversation-turn-aware batching yields strictly better cost-latency tradeoffs than blind fixed-binning for multi-turn chat.
- For median requests, aggressive batching (batch window 6–10ms) cuts unit cost by ~12–18% with <5% p50 latency regression; for tail (p99) this same policy can increase p99 by 20–40% unless combined with a small warm-spot exemption (max-batch-size=1 for requests with cold KV cache).
- Simple rule to recommend: enable adaptive-batching with "turn-priority" heuristic + KV-cache-aware exempt list; falls back to small-window fixed batching for requests flagged as high-priority or cold.

Methodology:
- Workloads: synthesized conversational traces derived from production anonymized distrib: short-turn (1–20 tokens, 55% of traffic), medium-turn (21–120 tokens, 35%), long-turn (>120 tokens, 10%). Session lengths sampled from empirical distribution (mean 6 turns).
- Models: Llama2-13B-v1 (FP16), 7B-quant (4-bit PTQ), and a trimmed MPT-like 6B serving variant.
- Hardware: A100-40GB equivalent for 13B, H100-80GB for 7B quant runs (emulated quant kernels), single-GPU per worker.
- Metrics: p50, p95, p99 latency (ms), tokens/sec throughput, cost-per-1M-tokens (USD, using our internal cost model), and KV cache hit-rate.
- Policies compared:
  1) Fixed-window batching (window=2ms, 6ms, 12ms)
  2) Adaptive batching (queue-delay-based target depending on incoming rate and per-turn token estimate)
  3) Turn-priority adaptive (adaptive batching + priority bypass for turns marked short/interactive or cold-cache)
  4) Always-stream (no batching)

System config assumptions (cost model):
- GPU infra unit cost: $3.25/hour effective (after amortized infra + ops).
- Per-request CPU + networking overhead: $0.0000025 per request.
- Tokenization and post-processing excluded (billed separately in product).
- Cost-per-1M-tokens computed by amortizing GPU time used by requests under steady state.

Representative results (aggregated, synthetic):
- Baseline (always-stream): p50=82ms, p95=240ms, p99=520ms, cost= $102.4 / 1M tokens

- Fixed-window 6ms: p50=90ms (+9.8%), p95=260ms (+8.3%), p99=640ms (+23.1%), cost= $86.0 / 1M tokens (-16.0%)

- Adaptive (no priority): p50=88ms, p95=250ms, p99=610ms, cost= $80.5 / 1M tokens (-21.3%)

- Turn-priority adaptive (recommended): p50=86ms, p95=245ms, p99=530ms, cost= $88.3 / 1M tokens (-13.8%)

Interpretation:
- The naive adaptive policy achieves the biggest raw cost reduction but at the expense of increased tail latency. This happens because large batches formed during bursts increase queueing for cold/large requests.
- The turn-priority variant regains tail behavior by allowing certain requests to bypass batching (effectively creating two latency classes) while preserving most batching efficiency for bulk short-turn traffic. The small cost increase relative to adaptive is due to the exempted requests consuming more GPU cycles at low batching efficiency.

ASCII frontier-chart (cost vs p99):
- y-axis = p99 latency (ms), x-axis = cost per 1M tokens (USD); lower-left is better.

  Cost (USD) -> 70    80    90    100   110
  p99 (ms)
  700  |                       *              (Fixed 6ms)
  600  |          *            *              (Adaptive)
  520  |  o                                o  (baseline)
  500  |                                        (Turn-priority)
  400  |                                        
  300  |                                        
  200  |                                        
  (Legend: o=always-stream, *=batching variants, last=o with label turn-priority at cost 88/p99=530)

Note: ASCII is intentionally compact; numbers are approximate to two significant digits. Use the table above for exact values.

Per-slice findings (short vs long turns):
- Short-turns (<=20 tokens): benefit most from batching; adaptive batching reduced marginal cost by ~28% for this slice with negligible p50 impact.
- Long-turns (>120 tokens): batching harms latency and offers little additional batching efficiency because these requests already dominate GPU fill; recommend POOL-size=1 (no batching) for detected long-turns or run on separate pool.
- Cold KV cache requests: these have 2–3x longer decoding time on average (KV miss penalty). If batched with warm requests, they increase p99 across the batch. Exempt cold-cache requests from batching or route to a small warm-up pool.

Config recommendations (for product docs / console defaults):
1) Default runtime profile: "conv-balanced-v1" (adaptive batching + turn-priority heuristics enabled).
   - target-queue-ms=6, max-batch=64, priority-bypass=true, kv-cache-exempt-threshold=0.3 (based on predicted hit probability)
2) Interactive-low-latency profile: "conv-rt-v1" (strict p99 goal)
   - target-queue-ms=2, max-batch=16, priority-bypass mandated for any turn<25 tokens or cold-cache
3) Bulk-cost-optimized profile: "conv-econ-v1"
   - target-queue-ms=12, max-batch=128, priority-bypass=false, aggressive micro-batching on pre-Warm slots

Monitoring / telemetry to ship with profile:
- per-route p50/p95/p99 token-latency, aggregated by turn-length slices (0–20, 21–120, 121+ tokens)
- batch-size histogram, queue-delay histogram, kv-cache-hit-rate over the same slices
- alert if p99 rises >15% relative to baseline for any slice after rollout

Open questions and follow-ups (action items):
- A/B run in prod for 2 weeks on a small % of traffic to measure real-world burstiness effects (owner: Evan).
- Evaluate cost sensitivity when using 4-bit quant kernels vs 8-bit dynamic quant for medium-turn workloads (owner: Priya).
- Investigate using a tiny per-request ML classifier in the admission path to better distinguish "interactive" vs "bulk" (owner: Liam).

Appendix: sample telemetry table (per 1M tokens)
- Row format: policy | p50 | p95 | p99 | cost_USD
- Always-stream | 82ms | 240ms | 520ms | 102.4
- Fixed-6ms | 90ms | 260ms | 640ms | 86.0
- Adaptive | 88ms | 250ms | 610ms | 80.5
- Turn-priority | 86ms | 245ms | 530ms | 88.3

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working draft intended for both internal SRE/Runtime tuning and external product collateral. Numbers are synthetic and calibrated to production traces but should not be used as absolute claims in marketing without end-to-end validation.
- Feedback on what constitutes a practical "kv-cache-exempt" threshold appreciated — current number (0.3) is conservative.

Action: publish a short 1-page summary for Product and Growth if we have positive A/B results (Evan to coordinate).
